name: Work across two clusters with contexts
objective: CKA exam-environment skill: every task names the cluster to target. Drill the whole multi-cluster surface harder than the exam — switch contexts, create on the right cluster (never the wrong one), set a context's default namespace, copy a live resource across clusters with get|apply, inspect contexts, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix of a resource built on the WRONG cluster. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Switch context and act on the right cluster
questions.teach:
`kubectl config use-context <name>` switches the **active context** — the cluster every later `kubectl` lands on. You have `kind-kindlab` (`$CTX`) and `kind-kindlab2` (`$CTX2`). Confirm with `kubectl config get-contexts`: the `*` marks the active one.

**Shell tip:** switching context stays in the *same shell*, so your `alias k` / `export do` **persist** across clusters — set them once. They only reset if you `ssh` to a node; add them to `~/.bashrc` to survive new terminal tabs.

**Gotcha:** a correct command on the wrong cluster grades wrong — this step requires `prod` on cluster2 and NOT on cluster1.
questions.prompt:
Switch to the **second** cluster and create namespace `prod` **there** (`$CTX2`), not on cluster1.

Target: namespace `prod` exists on cluster2 and does NOT exist on cluster1.
questions.hint: `kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab2` then `kubectl create namespace prod` — or one-shot: `kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 create ns prod`.
questions.solution:
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab2
kubectl create namespace prod
kubectl config get-contexts   # confirm the * is on kind-kindlab2
questions.eli5:
Think of `kubectl` as a TV remote, and each cluster as a different TV in the house. The remote can only talk to **one TV at a time** — whichever one it's currently pointed at. That "currently pointed at" setting is called the **active context**.

`kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab2` is you pointing the remote at the second TV. From then on, every button you press (`create`, `delete`, `get`) hits **that** TV until you point it somewhere else.

To check which TV you're aimed at, run `kubectl config get-contexts`. The one with a `*` next to it is the active one — like a little light showing where the remote is pointing.

So the whole move is: point the remote at cluster2, then press "create namespace prod." That namespace shows up on cluster2 and nowhere else.

**Watch out for:**

- **A perfect command on the wrong cluster is still wrong.** The grader checks *where* `prod` ended up. If you forget to switch, `prod` lands on cluster1 and you fail — even though the command "worked."
- **`use-context` sticks.** It writes to your kubeconfig file, so it stays switched even in a new shell. Don't assume you're on cluster1 just because you were a minute ago — check with the `*`.
- **Your shell aliases survive the switch.** Switching context is just a config change in the same shell, so `alias k` and `export do=...` keep working across both clusters. They only vanish if you `ssh` into a node.
- The context name is `kind-kindlab2`, not `kindlab2` — kind prefixes `kind-`.
questions.deepDive:
## Contexts & `use-context` — full rundown

### The mental model
A **kubeconfig** file ties together three kinds of entries, and a **context** is a named bundle that points at one of each:

- **cluster** — *where* the API server is (server URL + CA cert).
- **user** — *who* you authenticate as (cert/token/etc.).
- **context** — a named triple of **cluster + user + (optional) namespace**.

The **active context** (a.k.a. current-context) is the single context every bare `kubectl` command uses. Switching it is how you move between clusters in one shell.

### kubeconfig structure
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
current-context: kind-kindlab        # the active context
clusters:
- name: kind-kindlab
  cluster:
    server: https://127.0.0.1:6443
    certificate-authority-data: <base64>
users:
- name: kind-kindlab
  user:
    client-certificate-data: <base64>
    client-key-data: <base64>
contexts:
- name: kind-kindlab                 # the context name you pass to use-context
  context:
    cluster: kind-kindlab
    user: kind-kindlab
    namespace: default               # optional default namespace
```

> Note: the **context name** is arbitrary and independent of the cluster/user names it references. `kind` happens to name all three `kind-<clustername>`.

### The core commands
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `kubectl config get-contexts` | list all contexts; `*` marks the active one |
| `kubectl config current-context` | print just the active context name |
| `kubectl config use-context <name>` | switch the active context (writes to kubeconfig) |
| `kubectl config set-context <name> --namespace=<ns>` | change a context's default namespace |
| `kubectl config view` | print the merged kubeconfig |
| `kubectl config view --minify` | show only the active context's cluster/user/ns |
| `kubectl --context <name> <cmd>` | run ONE command against `<name>` without switching |

### Two ways to target a cluster
```bash
# A) Switch the active context, then run many commands on it
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab2
kubectl create namespace prod

# B) One-shot override — never touches the active context
kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 create namespace prod
```
Use **A** when you'll do several things on one cluster; use **B** for a single surgical command so you don't risk forgetting to switch back.

### Confirming where you are
```bash
kubectl config current-context          # -> kind-kindlab2
kubectl config get-contexts             # * on the active row
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Right command, wrong cluster = fail.** Grading checks the end state *on a specific cluster*. Always confirm the `*` before a bare create/delete.
- **`use-context` persists** to the kubeconfig file on disk, so the switch survives into a new shell/tab. Set it deliberately; don't assume.
- **`--context` overrides the active context** only for that one invocation and does **not** change `current-context`.
- **Context name vs cluster name:** you pass the *context* name to `use-context`. For kind it's `kind-<name>` (so `kind-kindlab2`, not `kindlab2`).
- Switching context is a same-shell config change — **shell aliases/env survive**; they only reset if you `ssh` to a node.
- Clusters are fully **independent**: creating an object on one never appears on the other.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl config get-contexts                 # see all; * = active
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab2     # switch
kubectl create namespace prod                # lands on the active cluster
kubectl config current-context               # verify
# one-shot alternative:
kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 create ns prod
```

questions.title: Deploy onto cluster2 (one safe command)
questions.teach:
Scope a single command to one cluster AND namespace with `--context` and `-n` together: `kubectl --context $CTX2 -n prod create deployment api --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2`. This never touches your active context.

**Gotcha:** omit `-n` and the Deployment lands in the context's default namespace (usually `default`), not the one you meant.
questions.prompt:
On cluster2, create a Deployment `api` (image `nginx:alpine`, 2 replicas) in the `prod` namespace.

Target: Deployment `api` with image `nginx:alpine` and 2 replicas exists in `prod` on cluster2.
questions.solution: kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create deployment api --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2

verification.description: Deployment 'api' (nginx:alpine, 2 replicas) in prod on cluster2

questions.eli5:
Imagine mailing a package. You don't have to *move house* to a new city just to send one parcel there — you can write the destination city **and** the exact street address right on the label, and it goes to that one place. Everything else about where *you* live stays the same.

That's what `--context` plus `-n` do on a single command:

- `--context kind-kindlab2` is the **city** (which cluster).
- `-n prod` is the **street address** (which namespace).

So `kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create deployment api --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2` drops the Deployment onto cluster2, into the `prod` namespace, in one shot — **without** changing your active context. The next command you type still goes wherever you were "living" before.

A **Deployment** just means "run N copies of this image and keep them alive." Here N is 2 (`--replicas=2`) and the image is `nginx:alpine`.

**Watch out for:**

- **Forget `-n` and it goes to the wrong room.** With no `-n`, the Deployment lands in the context's **default namespace** (usually `default`), not `prod`. The command still "succeeds" — it's just in the wrong place.
- **`--context` doesn't switch you.** It only affects this one command. Handy, but it also means you can't rely on it having changed anything for your *next* command.
- The image must be exactly `nginx:alpine` and replicas exactly `2` — grading is precise.
- Order doesn't matter, but both flags go **before** the `create` verb's resource args work cleanly; keep `--context` and `-n` up front.
questions.deepDive:
## Scoping one command to a cluster + namespace — full rundown ### The mental model Every `kubectl` command resolves **three things**: which cluster, which identity, which namespace. Normally they come from the active context. But you can **override** them per-command with flags — the override wins for that invocation only and never edits the kubeconfig. | Flag | Overrides | Example | |---|---|---| | `--context ` | cluster + user (the whole context) | `--context kind-kindlab2` | | `-n` / `--namespace ` | the namespace | `-n prod` | | `--cluster` / `--user` | just the cluster or just the user | rarely needed | | `--kubeconfig ` | which kubeconfig file to read | `--kubeconfig ~/alt.conf` | Combine `--context` and `-n` to hit exactly one cluster + namespace in a single safe command, leaving your active context untouched. ### The task pattern ```bash kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod \ create deployment api --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2 ``` - `--context kind-kindlab2` → cluster2 - `-n prod` → the `prod` namespace - `create deployment api ...` → the imperative create ### Imperative `create deployment` | Part | Meaning | |---|---| | `create deployment ` | make a Deployment named `` | | `--image=` | container image for the pod template | | `--replicas=` | desired pod count (default 1 if omitted) | | `--port=

` | optional containerPort | | `--dry-run=client -o yaml` | print the manifest instead of applying | A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which keeps `replicas` pods running and supports rolling updates. ```bash # generate YAML to inspect/edit before applying kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create deployment api \ --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2 --dry-run=client -o yaml ``` ### Verifying ```bash kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod get deploy api kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod get deploy api \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}{" "}{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'; echo ``` ### Flag precedence (highest wins) 1. Explicit per-command flags (`--context`, `-n`, `--kubeconfig`) 2. The active context's values (cluster/user/namespace) 3. Built-in defaults (namespace `default`) ### Gotchas & exam traps - **Omitting `-n` ≠ error.** The Deployment silently lands in the context's default namespace (often `default`). Always set `-n` when the task names a namespace. - **`--context` does not persist.** It scopes one command; `current-context` is unchanged afterward. - **`--replicas` default is 1.** If the task wants 2, you must pass it; `create deployment` won't infer it. - If the namespace doesn't exist yet, `create` fails with `namespaces "prod" not found` — create the namespace first (prior step). - `-n` affects **namespaced** resources only; cluster-scoped objects (nodes, namespaces, PVs) ignore it. ### Quick reference ```bash kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create deployment api \ --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2 kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod get deploy api # confirm ```

questions.title: Now work on cluster1
questions.teach:
Switching back to cluster1 is just another `use-context kind-kindlab`. Create a ConfigMap imperatively: `kubectl create configmap <name> --from-literal=key=value`.

**Gotcha:** the clusters are fully independent — the ConfigMap you make on cluster1 does NOT exist on cluster2.
questions.prompt:
Switch to **cluster1** (`$CTX`) and create a ConfigMap `shared-cfg` with key `env=prod` in the `default` namespace **there**.

Target: `shared-cfg` (env=prod) exists in default on cluster1 and NOT in default on cluster2.
questions.hint: `kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab` then `kubectl create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod`.
questions.solution:
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab
kubectl create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod

verification.description: configmap 'shared-cfg' (env=prod) in default on cluster1 only

questions.eli5:
Picture two separate **filing cabinets**, one for each cluster. They look identical, but they share nothing — a folder you drop into cabinet 1 does **not** magically appear in cabinet 2. They're independent.

This step is two small moves:

1. **Point the remote back at cluster1:** `kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab`. Earlier you switched to cluster2; now you come home.
2. **File a note.** A **ConfigMap** is just a little named bag of key/value settings — plain configuration you want your apps to read. You make one quickly with `kubectl create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod`, which means "create a ConfigMap called `shared-cfg` holding `env=prod`."

Because you're pointed at cluster1 and didn't say otherwise, it lands in the `default` namespace on cluster1 — and only there.

**Watch out for:**

- **The clusters don't sync.** `shared-cfg` on cluster1 does **not** exist on cluster2. The grader actually checks it's *absent* from cluster2, so don't accidentally create it twice.
- **Did you really switch back?** If you skip the `use-context` and you're still on cluster2, the ConfigMap lands on the wrong cluster. Check the `*` with `kubectl config get-contexts`.
- **`--from-literal` wants `key=value`**, not a space. It's `env=prod`, and you can repeat the flag for more keys.
- No namespace flag here means `default` — which is exactly what this task wants, but be aware the default comes from the context.
questions.deepDive:
## Switching back + imperative ConfigMaps — full rundown

### The mental model
Two clusters are two **independent** state stores. Nothing replicates between them automatically. "Working on cluster1" means your active context (or `--context`) points at cluster1, and every object you create lives only there.

Switching back is nothing special — it's the same `use-context` you used to leave:
```bash
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab
```

### Creating a ConfigMap imperatively
A **ConfigMap** stores non-secret key/value configuration that pods consume as env vars, command-line args, or mounted files.

```bash
kubectl create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod
```

| Source flag | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `--from-literal=K=V` | inline key/value (repeatable) | `--from-literal=env=prod --from-literal=tier=web` |
| `--from-file=path` | file contents; key = filename | `--from-file=app.properties` |
| `--from-file=K=path` | file contents under a chosen key | `--from-file=cfg=./app.properties` |
| `--from-env-file=path` | each `K=V` line becomes a key | `--from-env-file=.env` |

Resulting object:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: shared-cfg
  namespace: default
data:
  env: prod
```

### Verifying
```bash
kubectl get configmap shared-cfg -o yaml
kubectl get configmap shared-cfg -o jsonpath='{.data.env}'; echo   # -> prod
kubectl describe configmap shared-cfg
```

### Namespace resolution
With no `-n`, the ConfigMap lands in the **context's default namespace**. If the context hasn't set one, that's `default`. To be explicit:
```bash
kubectl -n default create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Confirm the active context first.** If you didn't switch back, the ConfigMap lands on cluster2. `kubectl config current-context` before you create.
- **Clusters don't propagate.** The object exists only on the cluster you targeted; grading may check it's *absent* on the other one.
- **`--from-literal` syntax is `key=value`** (no spaces, no quotes needed for simple values). Repeat the flag for multiple keys.
- ConfigMaps are **namespaced** — a pod can only mount a ConfigMap in its own namespace.
- `create configmap` fails if one with that name already exists; use `kubectl create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -` to be idempotent.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab                 # back to cluster1
kubectl create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod
kubectl get configmap shared-cfg -o jsonpath='{.data.env}'; echo
```

questions.title: Copy a live resource across clusters (get | apply)
questions.teach:
To clone an object onto another cluster, pipe it: `kubectl --context $CTX get configmap shared-cfg -o yaml | kubectl --context $CTX2 -n prod apply -f -`.

**Gotcha:** a raw `get -o yaml` carries `resourceVersion`/`uid`/`namespace` — override the target with `-n prod` on apply, or just recreate imperatively.
questions.prompt:
Replicate `shared-cfg` (env=prod) from cluster1 into the `prod` namespace on **cluster2** — same key/value.

Target: ConfigMap `shared-cfg` with `env=prod` exists in `prod` on cluster2.
questions.hint: Simplest that always works: `kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod`. Or pipe `get -o yaml` from cluster1 into `apply -f -` on cluster2 with `-n prod`.
questions.solution: kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod

verification.description: shared-cfg (env=prod) exists in prod on cluster2

questions.eli5:
Say you have a recipe card in your kitchen (cluster1) and you want the same recipe in a friend's kitchen (cluster2). Two ways to do it:

1. **Photocopy and hand it over.** Read the card from cluster1 and feed that copy straight into cluster2:
   `kubectl --context $CTX get configmap shared-cfg -o yaml | kubectl --context $CTX2 -n prod apply -f -`
   The `|` pipe is the hand-off: the left side *reads*, the right side *writes*.

2. **Just rewrite it by hand.** Since it's only `env=prod`, the simplest, always-works move is to create it fresh on cluster2:
   `kubectl --context $CTX2 -n prod create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod`

Both get you the same ConfigMap in `prod` on cluster2.

**Watch out for:**

- **A raw `get -o yaml` carries baggage.** The exported YAML includes fields tied to the *original* cluster — `resourceVersion`, `uid`, `creationTimestamp`, and the old `namespace`. If you `apply` it blindly, the stale `namespace` can send it to the wrong place.
- **Override the namespace on apply.** Adding `-n prod` on the right side of the pipe forces it into `prod` regardless of what the YAML says — usually enough. (For fussier objects you'd strip the baggage, but `-n` handles the namespace.)
- **`apply -f -`** — the trailing `-` means "read the file from stdin," i.e. from the pipe. Forget it and apply has nothing to read.
- **The target namespace must already exist** on cluster2, or apply/create fails.
- When in doubt, just **recreate imperatively** — no baggage, no surprises.

## Copying a live resource across clusters — full rundown

### The mental model
There's no built-in "copy object from cluster A to cluster B." You do it by **exporting** from the source and **applying** to the target. Because `kubectl` can target either cluster via `--context`, you can chain both ends in one pipeline.

```bash
kubectl --context kind-kindlab  get configmap shared-cfg -o yaml \
| kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod apply -f -
```
- Left side: read the object from cluster1 as YAML.
- `|` : pass that YAML to the next command's stdin.
- Right side: `apply -f -` reads from stdin (`-`) and creates/updates on cluster2, forced into `-n prod`.

### What a raw `get -o yaml` includes (and why it matters)
An exported object carries **cluster-specific, server-managed fields** that shouldn't be reused:

| Field | Problem when re-applied |
|---|---|
| `metadata.uid` | unique to the source cluster/object |
| `metadata.resourceVersion` | causes conflicts / is meaningless on target |
| `metadata.creationTimestamp` | server-assigned |
| `metadata.namespace` | points at the *source* namespace |
| `status:` | server-owned, not spec |

`apply` tolerates most of these (it ignores/overwrites server fields), but the stale **namespace** is the one that bites you — override it with `-n` on the target command.

### Three reliable approaches
```bash
# A) Pipe get|apply, override namespace on the target
kubectl --context kind-kindlab get cm shared-cfg -o yaml \
| kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod apply -f -

# B) Clean the YAML first (portable manifest)
kubectl --context kind-kindlab get cm shared-cfg -o yaml \
  | kubectl neat 2>/dev/null \
  | kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod apply -f -
# (no kubectl-neat? strip fields by hand or use C)

# C) Simplest & bulletproof for small objects — just recreate
kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create configmap shared-cfg \
  --from-literal=env=prod
```

### `apply` vs `create` here
- **`create`** — fails if the object already exists; no stale fields; great for simple imperative recreation.
- **`apply`** — declarative; creates or updates; needed when consuming piped YAML (`-f -`).

### Reading from stdin
`-f -` tells `kubectl` to read the manifest from **stdin** (the pipe). Omit the `-` and there's nothing to apply.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Stale `namespace` in exported YAML** → object lands in the wrong namespace. Override with `-n` on apply, or edit the YAML.
- **Target namespace must exist** before apply/create, else `namespaces "prod" not found`.
- **Secrets copy the same way**, but values are base64 in `data:` — a plain `get -o yaml | apply` preserves them fine.
- **`status` and server fields** are harmless with `apply` but will clutter a saved manifest — clean them for reusable files.
- For anything non-trivial, **recreating imperatively** avoids all baggage — prefer it when the object is simple.

### Quick reference
```bash
# cross-cluster clone via pipe
kubectl --context kind-kindlab get cm shared-cfg -o yaml \
| kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod apply -f -

# or just recreate
kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create cm shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod
kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod get cm shared-cfg -o jsonpath='{.data.env}'; echo
```

questions.title: Set a context's default namespace
questions.teach:
A context pins cluster+user+**namespace**. Set the default namespace so you stop typing `-n`: `kubectl config set-context kind-kindlab2 --namespace=prod`. Now bare commands on that context hit `prod`.

**Gotcha:** `set-context --current` edits whatever is active now — name the context explicitly (`kind-kindlab2`) so you edit the right one regardless of where you're standing.
questions.prompt:
Set the **default namespace** of the `$CTX2` context to `prod` (so `kubectl --context $CTX2 get pods` with no `-n` targets `prod`).

Target: context `kind-kindlab2` has `namespace: prod` in the kubeconfig.
questions.hint: `kubectl config set-context kind-kindlab2 --namespace=prod`. Confirm with `kubectl config get-contexts` (NAMESPACE column).
questions.solution:
kubectl config set-context kind-kindlab2 --namespace=prod
kubectl config get-contexts
questions.eli5:
Every context is like a saved GPS "home address" for your remote: it remembers which cluster, which user, **and** which room (namespace) you usually want. Until now the room was `default`, so you kept typing `-n prod` every single time to redirect.

`kubectl config set-context kind-kindlab2 --namespace=prod` changes that saved home address so the `prod` room is the default. After this, a bare `kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 get pods` (no `-n`) automatically looks in `prod`. Less typing, fewer mistakes.

Think of it as updating your food-delivery app's saved address from "home" to "office" — now every order goes to the office unless you say otherwise.

**Watch out for:**

- **Name the context explicitly.** There's a tempting shortcut, `set-context --current`, which edits *whatever context is active right now*. If you're standing on the wrong cluster, you'll edit the wrong context's address. Writing `kind-kindlab2` by name edits the right one no matter where you're standing.
- **This only changes a default, not permissions.** Setting the namespace doesn't create it — `prod` must already exist, and you still need access to it.
- **`set-context` edits the kubeconfig file**, so the change sticks across shells and tabs.
- **Confirm it took.** Run `kubectl config get-contexts` and check the **NAMESPACE** column for that row says `prod`.
- A bare command *still* obeys an explicit `-n` if you add one — the default only applies when you leave `-n` off.
questions.deepDive:
## Setting a context's default namespace — full rundown

### The mental model
A context is `cluster + user + namespace`. The **namespace** field is the default that bare (no `-n`) commands use on that context. Setting it means you stop typing `-n prod` for every command on cluster2.

```bash
kubectl config set-context kind-kindlab2 --namespace=prod
```

This edits the `contexts[].context.namespace` field in the kubeconfig:
```yaml
contexts:
- name: kind-kindlab2
  context:
    cluster: kind-kindlab2
    user: kind-kindlab2
    namespace: prod        # <- set by the command
```

### `set-context` forms
| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `kubectl config set-context <name> --namespace=<ns>` | set default ns on a **named** context |
| `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns>` | set default ns on the **active** context |
| `kubectl config set-context <name> --cluster=<c> --user=<u>` | create/repoint a context's cluster/user |
| `kubectl config set-context <name>` | create a bare context entry |

### `--current` vs naming the context
- `--current` edits whatever `current-context` is **right now** — convenient but dangerous if you're not sure where you're standing.
- Passing the **explicit name** (`kind-kindlab2`) edits that exact context regardless of the active one. Prefer this for determinism (and for grading).

### Verifying
```bash
kubectl config get-contexts                 # NAMESPACE column shows 'prod' for kind-kindlab2
kubectl config view --minify --context kind-kindlab2 \
  -o jsonpath='{.contexts[0].context.namespace}'; echo
# functional check:
kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 get pods    # no -n → targets prod now
```

### How namespace is resolved (precedence)
1. Explicit `-n`/`--namespace` on the command (highest)
2. The context's `namespace` field (what you just set)
3. `default` if neither is set

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Setting the namespace does not create it.** `prod` must already exist; this only changes a default.
- **`--current` edits the active context** — if you switched clusters earlier you may edit the wrong one. Name the context explicitly.
- **It persists** to the kubeconfig file (survives new shells).
- An explicit `-n` on a later command still **overrides** the default — the default only applies when `-n` is omitted.
- Changing the default namespace does **not** move existing objects; it only affects where future bare commands look.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl config set-context kind-kindlab2 --namespace=prod

```

questions.deepDive:
## Secrets & cluster independence — full rundown

### The mental model
A **Secret** holds small sensitive data (passwords, tokens, keys, certs). It's structurally like a ConfigMap but intended for confidential values and treated slightly specially by the API (not shown in plain `describe`, can be encrypted at rest, mounted tmpfs). Like all objects, it lives in **one namespace on one cluster** — nothing replicates across clusters.

### Imperative creation
```bash
kubectl --context kind-kindlab -n default create secret generic db-cred \
  --from-literal=password=s3cr3t
```

### Secret types
| Type | Command | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `generic` (Opaque) | `create secret generic` | arbitrary key/values via `--from-literal`/`--from-file` |
| `tls` | `create secret tls <name> --cert=... --key=...` | TLS cert + key (`kubernetes.io/tls`) |
| `docker-registry` | `create secret docker-registry ...` | image pull credentials (`kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`) |

### `generic` source flags (same as ConfigMap)
| Flag | Example |
|---|---|
| `--from-literal=K=V` | `--from-literal=password=s3cr3t` (repeatable) |
| `--from-file=path` | key = filename, value = contents |
| `--from-file=K=path` | value under chosen key |
| `--from-env-file=path` | each `K=V` line → a key |

Resulting object (note base64):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-cred
  namespace: default
type: Opaque
data:
  password: czNjcjN0        # base64("s3cr3t")
```

### Inspecting / decoding
```bash
kubectl get secret db-cred -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; echo   # -> s3cr3t
kubectl get secret db-cred -o yaml
# Decode-free view (1.30+):
kubectl get secret db-cred -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode
```

### base64 is NOT encryption
`data` values are base64-encoded only. Anyone with read access can decode them. Real confidentiality requires **encryption at rest** (`EncryptionConfiguration` on the API server) and/or RBAC limiting who can `get` Secrets.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`generic` keyword is mandatory**: `create secret generic` — other types take different flags.
- **Values are base64, not encrypted** — a classic exam "gotcha" question.
- **No cross-cluster sync** — creating on cluster1 does not appear on cluster2; grading may verify absence on the other cluster.
- **`--from-literal=key=value`** (no spaces). Repeat for multiple keys.
- Secrets are **namespaced**; a pod can only reference a Secret in its own namespace.
- Confirm the active/target cluster — a correct command on the wrong cluster grades wrong.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl --context kind-kindlab -n default create secret generic db-cred \
  --from-literal=password=s3cr3t
kubectl --context kind-kindlab -n default get secret db-cred \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; echo    # s3cr3t
```

questions.title: Context discipline — know where you are
questions.teach:
Finish each task by leaving your active context where the *next* one expects, then verify with `kubectl config current-context`. Set it back to cluster1 with `kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab`.

**Gotcha:** `use-context` persists to the kubeconfig file, so your choice survives into the next task's shell — set it deliberately rather than assuming.
questions.prompt:
Leave your **active** context set to cluster1 (`$CTX`).

Target: `kubectl config current-context` returns `kind-kindlab`.
questions.solution:
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab
kubectl config current-context   # kind-kindlab
questions.eli5:
When you're driving a forklift between two warehouses, the golden rule is: **always know which warehouse you're parked in before you unload.** Most warehouse accidents happen because someone *assumed* they were in building A when they were actually in building B.

Same with clusters. This step is about **discipline**: before you move on, deliberately leave your active context where the next task expects it, then double-check.

- Set it back to cluster1: `kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab`.
- Confirm out loud: `kubectl config current-context` should print `kind-kindlab`.

That's it — no object to create, just making sure the remote is pointed where it should be so the next person (or the next task, or future-you) doesn't get surprised.

**Watch out for:**

- **Your choice persists.** `use-context` writes to the kubeconfig on disk, so whatever you leave it on carries into the next task's shell. That's exactly why you set it *deliberately* instead of hoping.
- **Don't confuse `current-context` with `--context`.** `current-context` *reports/sets* the active one; `--context` only overrides a single command and changes nothing permanent.
- **`get-contexts` shows all, `current-context` shows one.** Use `current-context` for a clean, scriptable check (it prints just the name).
- The target is exactly `kind-kindlab` — the cluster1 context name, with the `kind-` prefix.
questions.deepDive:
## Context discipline — knowing where you are — full rundown

### The mental model
In a multi-cluster exam, the single biggest source of silent failures is acting on the **wrong active context**. "Context discipline" = a habit loop: **check → act → leave it where the next task expects**. The active context persists to disk, so it's your responsibility to set it deliberately, not assume.

### The inspection commands
| Command | Output | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| `kubectl config current-context` | just the active context name | fast scriptable check / grading |
| `kubectl config get-contexts` | table of all contexts; `*` = active | see everything + namespaces |
| `kubectl config view --minify` | full config for the active context only | verify cluster/user/ns details |
| `kubectl config get-contexts -o name` | names only | scripting |

### Setting / leaving the context
```bash
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab     # make cluster1 active (persists to kubeconfig)
kubectl config current-context              # -> kind-kindlab  (verify)
```

### Active context vs per-command override
- **`use-context <name>`** changes `current-context` in the kubeconfig — **persistent**, affects all future bare commands and survives new shells.
- **`--context <name>`** overrides for **one** command only; `current-context` is unchanged. Great for surgical actions without disturbing where you're "standing."

### A reliable workflow
```bash
# 1. Know where you are
kubectl config current-context
# 2. Go where the task says
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab2
# 3. Do the work (bare commands now hit cluster2)
# 4. Leave it where the NEXT task expects
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab
kubectl config current-context              # confirm before moving on
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Persistence cuts both ways:** the context you leave behind is where the next shell starts. Set it on purpose.
- **`current-context` can error** (`error: current-context is not set`) if no active context — set one with `use-context`.
- **Don't rely on `--context` to "leave" a state** — it changes nothing permanent. Use `use-context` to actually move the active pointer.
- **Name precision:** kind context names are `kind-<cluster>` (`kind-kindlab`, `kind-kindlab2`).
- Prefer **`current-context`** over parsing `get-contexts` when you want a clean, single-value check.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl config current-context              # where am I?
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab     # set active = cluster1
kubectl config current-context              # verify -> kind-kindlab
kubectl config get-contexts                 # full picture, * = active
```
